summary: This Standards Track document defines transport mechanisms for moving CMC messages: HTTP, file, mail, and TCP. It obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402.

plainLanguage.summary:
This document is about the plumbing under a certificate request. The same message can travel four ways: as a file on disk, as an email, as an HTTP request, or as raw bytes down a TCP connection.

Each way has its own conventions. Files get a standard extension so everyone can tell what is inside. Mail gets a content type so the receiving server knows how to parse it. HTTP uses a POST and expects a success code. The TCP option is the simplest, with a registered port number and no wrapping at all.

subtitle: Four ways to carry a certificate request between a client and a certificate authority.

tldr.problem: A certificate management message has to travel from the client asking for a certificate to the authority that issues it, and back. The message format says nothing about how to move it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes four transports. Files can carry a request for an offline client, mail can carry one as a message with the right content type, HTTP can carry one with a POST, and a plain TCP connection can carry the bytes with no wrapping at all.
tldr.outcome: Each transport has its own rules for naming files and setting content types, and the TCP option now has a registered port, 5318. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402 and replaces the older TLS rules with the current guidance.

today: RFC 10003 is a Proposed Standard from July 2026. It obsoletes RFC 5273 and RFC 6402, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The document is one of three parts of the specification, alongside the message structure and the requirements usage documents.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
This document defines a number of transport methods used to move CMC messages, which are defined in the companion structure document. The transports described are HTTP, file, mail and TCP. It obsoletes the earlier transport document and the earlier update document, and it also incorporates one erratum against the earlier transport document.

The document is short because the message format itself is defined elsewhere. All it has to say is how the bytes get from one end to the other, and what each transport requires of the sender and the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything here is about getting the message across. What is in the message is someone else's problem.

sections.title: The File-Based Protocol
sections.content:
Enrollment messages and responses may be transferred between clients and servers using file-system mechanisms, such as when enrollment is performed for an offline client. When files are used to transport Full PKI Request or Full PKI Response messages, there must be only one instance of a request or response message in a single file, and the file must be binary encoded.

The abbreviations crq and crp stand for Full PKI Request and Full PKI Response respectively, and file extensions are defined for them. The extensions that should be used are .p10 for a Simple PKI Request, .crq for a Full PKI Request, .p7c for a Simple PKI Response and .crp for a Full PKI Response.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying a file onto a memory stick works for a client that cannot reach the network. The file name says what is inside, and there is only one message per file.

sections.title: The Mail-Based Protocol
sections.content:
MIME wrapping is defined for environments that support it, and the basic wrapping is taken from the S/MIME message specification. When using a mail-based protocol, MIME wrapping between the layers of the CMS wrapping is optional. The document notes that this is different from the standard S/MIME message.

The headers discussed below appear in the top-level content of the messages, and the messages' contents are the entire bodies. A set of simple request and response messages and a set of full request and response messages follow, each with an example.

Simple enrollment requests are encoded using the application/pkcs10 content type, and a file name must be included either in a Content-Type or a Content-Disposition header, in the name or filename parameter respectively. The extension for the file must be .p10. Simple PKI Response messages must be encoded as the content type application/pkcs7-mime, with a smime-type parameter on the Content-Type header with the value certs-only, and a file name with the .p7c extension. Full PKI Request messages must be encoded as application/pkcs7-mime with the smime-type parameter CMC-Request and the .p7m extension. Full PKI Response messages must be encoded as application/pkcs7-mime with the smime-type parameter CMC-Response and the .p7m extension.

For file names present in the name or filename parameters, non-ASCII text is prohibited.
sections.plainLanguage: An email carrying a certificate request looks like any other email, but the content type tells the receiving server what it is holding: a bare request, a full request, or a reply. The MIME wrapping on top of the message format is optional.

sections.title: The HTTP-Based Protocol
sections.content:
The HTTP transport follows the rules of the HTTP specification, and using HTTPS provides the content protection needed against eavesdroppers. For clients and servers to interoperate, clients are configured with enough information to form the server URI, and client requests are submitted with the POST method. Servers must use the 2XX response codes for successful responses.

Clients may attempt to send certification requests over HTTPS. Servers are not required to support TLS or QUIC, but a secure channel might be available depending on the HTTP version implemented. If TLS is used by the HTTP version, the implementation must follow the recommendations in the current best current practice on TLS. Implementations that support TLS 1.3 or QUIC must not use early data, that is 0-RTT, because POST is not idempotent.

Clients are not required to support any type of HTTP authentication or cookies, so servers cannot rely on those features being available. Clients and servers are expected to follow other rules and restrictions in HTTP, and only the rules that apply to POST are relevant here.

A request sent with the POST method has a Content-Type field with the value for a full request, and the body is the binary value of the encoding of the request. A response has a Content-Type field with the value for a full response, and the body is the binary value of the basic encoding rules encoding of either a simple or a full response.
sections.plainLanguage: The request goes out as an HTTP POST and the answer comes back as the body of the reply. Because a POST repeats badly, the early-data shortcut that newer TLS versions offer cannot be used here.

sections.title: The TCP-Based Protocol
sections.content:
When CMC messages are sent over a TCP-based connection, no wrapping is required of the message; messages are sent in their binary encoded form.

The client closes a connection after receiving a response, or it issues another request to the server using the same connection. Reusing one connection for multiple successive requests, instead of opening multiple connections that are only used for a single request, is recommended for performance and resource conservation reasons. The client must wait for the full response before making another request on the same connection. A server may close a connection after it has been idle for some period of time, and this timeout would typically be several minutes long.

CMC requires a registered port number to send and receive messages over TCP. The service name is pkix-cmc and the TCP port number is 5318. Before the earlier update document, CMC had no registered port number and used an externally configured port from the private port range. Client implementations may continue to use a port chosen from the private port range, but a server should use the port assigned to the CMC service, 5318. It is expected that HTTP will continue to be the primary transport method used by CMC installations.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the plainest option: the bytes of the message go down the connection as they are. A client may keep the connection open and send more requests on it, but it has to wait for each answer first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms for thwarting replay attacks may be required in particular implementations, depending on the operational environment. Where the certification authority maintains significant state information, replay attacks may be detectable without the optional nonce mechanisms. Implementers need to consider their environment carefully before choosing whether to use the sender and recipient nonce attributes, and developers of state-constrained clients are strongly encouraged to incorporate them.

Setting up a secure channel between an end entity and a certification authority or registration authority, and likewise between one authority and another, necessarily requires an out-of-band trust initiation mechanism. A secure channel may be built with IPsec or TLS, and the choice of any particular scheme is outside the scope of the document. Implementers are strongly encouraged to consider generally accepted principles of secure key management when integrating this capability within an overall security architecture.

In some instances no out-of-band trust will have been initiated before the protocol is used. This can occur when the protocol itself is used to download the set of trust anchors the protocols will use. In those instances the enveloped data or authenticated enveloped data content type provides the same shrouding that TLS would have provided.

For the mail-based protocol, those content types can also be used to apply confidentiality protection to the conveyed messages. Even if the application uses SMTP over TLS with its preferred message submission agent for the initial submission, SMTP in subsequent relay hops may not be either authenticated or encrypted. For some combinations of initial submission agent and destination domains it may be possible to request authenticated TLS at every relay hop through the mechanism in the relevant specification. This may be used when supported and expected to work, but it risks non-delivery if some of the servers along the relay chain do not support that extension.

For the file-based protocol, filesystem permissions are usually the way to apply confidentiality protection, by limiting read access to a single user or group corresponding to the entity authorised to read the request or response. Diligent use of those permissions can be a useful mechanism in multi-user environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Each transport has its own confidentiality story. Files rely on who can read the directory, mail relies on the encryption inside the message because the relay hops may be neither private nor authenticated, and the TCP and HTTP options rely on a secure channel that has to be set up separately.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Earlier Version
sections.content:
The document merges the text of the earlier update document. IANA assigned TCP port 5318 for the use of CMC. The file extensions for Full PKI Requests and Responses were clarified, and examples of encoding types were added for the mail-based requests and responses.

TLS 1.0 was replaced with TLS 1.2 or later, and implementations are required to follow the recommendations in the current best current practice on TLS. The use of early data was restricted where TLS 1.3 or QUIC is used, and the use of TCP pipelining was restricted. The limitations of SMTP over TLS and the use of authenticated TLS for message delivery were clarified. The erratum against the earlier transport document was addressed, and a reference was added to the HTTP implementation guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The main change is the arrival of a registered port number. The rest is the modernising of the TLS rules and a few clarifications about file names and mail encoding.

viz.caption: The rules for the HTTP transport

items.title: POST only
items.text: Client requests are submitted with the POST method.

items.title: 2XX for success
items.text: Servers must use the 2XX response codes for successful responses.

items.title: TLS follows the current guidance
items.text: Where TLS is used by the HTTP version, the implementation must follow the recommendations in the current best current practice on TLS.

items.title: No early data
items.text: Implementations that support TLS 1.3 or QUIC must not use early data, because POST is not idempotent.

items.title: No cookies or authentication
items.text: Clients are not required to support any type of HTTP authentication or cookies, so servers cannot rely on them.

viz.caption: The rules for the TCP transport

items.title: No wrapping
items.text: Messages are sent in their binary encoded form, with no additional wrapping.

items.title: Reuse the connection
items.text: The client closes the connection after a response or issues another request on the same connection. Reusing one connection is recommended for performance and resource conservation.

items.title: Wait for the full reply
items.text: The client must wait for the full response before making another request on the same connection.

items.title: A registered port
items.text: The service name is pkix-cmc and the port number is 5318. Servers should use it, and HTTP is expected to remain the primary transport.

viz.caption: How each transport keeps the message private

items.title: Replay attacks
items.text: Mechanisms against replay may be needed depending on the environment, and where the authority keeps little state the sender and recipient nonce attributes are worth using.

items.title: Trust has to be arranged separately
items.text: Setting up a secure channel between the client and the authority, or between one authority and another, needs an out-of-band trust mechanism such as IPsec or TLS.

items.title: Mail is not private all the way
items.text: Even with SMTP over TLS for the first hop, later relay hops may be neither authenticated nor encrypted, and asking for authenticated TLS at every hop risks non-delivery if some servers do not support it.

items.title: Files and permissions
items.text: For the file-based protocol, filesystem permissions are usually the way to keep a message confidential, by limiting read access to the entity entitled to read it.

items.title: Merged the update document
items.text: The text of the earlier update document is merged in.

items.title: A registered port
items.text: IANA assigned TCP port 5318 for CMC.

items.title: Newer TLS
items.text: TLS 1.0 was replaced with TLS 1.2 or later, and implementations are required to follow the recommendations in the current best current practice on TLS.

items.title: Restricted early data
items.text: Early data is restricted where TLS 1.3 or QUIC is used.

items.title: Restricted pipelining
items.text: The use of TCP pipelining was restricted.

items.title: Clearer names and examples
items.text: The file extensions for full requests and responses were clarified and encoding examples were added for the mail-based messages.
